html:
The Algonquin are an Indigenous people of the Ottawa River valley, on today's border of Ontario and Quebec. They speak a language closely related to Ojibwe, part of the large Algonquian family that is named after them.

They lived by hunting, fishing and gathering, and some groups grew maize. The Ottawa River was a great trade route, and the Algonquin charged other peoples to pass along it. In 1609 they, with the Wendat and the Innu, took Samuel de Champlain south to fight the Mohawk, which bound New France to them and set the French against the Haudenosaunee for a century. The Beaver Wars of the 1600s drove many Algonquin from the valley. Most Algonquin communities today never signed a land treaty with Canada. See Omàmiwininiwak.
